pinterest.title: Portuguese Wedding Traditions in Order, from the Asking to the Feast
pinterest.description: Portuguese wedding traditions follow a clear order: the pedido de casamento and noivado, choosing the padrinhos, the enxoval, then the copo-d'água feast and music from folk dances to Fado. This guide separates what dictionaries, UNESCO and official registries record from what is only often told, and covers what Australians need to marry legally in Portugal.

pinterest.title: Portuguese Wedding Traditions: The Minho Bride and Viana Gold Filigree
pinterest.description: In the Viana do Castelo area of the Minho, the traditional bridal costume is often described as black, worn with embroidery and layered gold. Filigree is often worn with it in northern Portugal, and the Coração de Viana began as a devotional symbol of the Sacred Heart of Jesus rather than a love token. Wearing a family heirloom? Plan your neckline around the piece.

pinterest.title: Who Are the Padrinhos? A Traditional Portuguese Wedding Explained
pinterest.description: In Portuguese, a padrinho is defined as the person who serves as a witness at a wedding, so choosing the padrinhos is a real role at the ceremony rather than an honorary title. At a civil ceremony in Portugal, two to four witnesses may take part, but they are not compulsory. Families can still choose padrinhos for meaning. Read the full guide to Portuguese wedding traditions.

slides: Portuguese wedding traditions you did not know, in the order they happen
The asking: the pedido de casamento. Traditionally, the groom or his family asks the bride's family for their blessing (often told). The engagement is the noivado.
The padrinhos: by dictionary definition, wedding witnesses. Choosing them is a real role at the ceremony, not an honorary title.
The enxoval: the clothes and linens a bride carries into married life. A grandmother's linen under the cake keeps the idea alive today.
The Minho bride: in the Viana do Castelo area, the bridal costume is often described as black, worn with embroidery and layered gold filigree.
The copo-d'água: the Portuguese name for the reception, literally "glass of water". Late in the night, caldo verde for the guests still dancing (often told).
Music: Fado and Cante Alentejano are both recognised by UNESCO. Neither is a wedding tradition, but a single song can mark the day.
Blending Portuguese customs into your day, here or in Portugal? Message us or speak with a Wedded Advisor about the paperwork and the plan.
instagram_carousel.caption:
Ask a Portuguese grandmother about her wedding and she will talk about her padrinhos, the linen she carried into married life and the gold at her throat before she mentions the dress.

Our new guide follows a Portuguese wedding in order, from the pedido de casamento to the copo-d'água feast, and separates what dictionaries, UNESCO and official registries record from what is only often told.

Customs vary by region, family and faith. The Minho bride and Viana gold belong to the north, and you are unlikely to see them at a wedding in Lisbon or the south.

Planning to marry legally in Portugal? Australians need a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage, which the embassy says takes at least four weeks, before the registry's process of at least one month.

Which customs did your family keep? Tell us in the comments, or tap the link in our bio to read the full guide and speak with a Wedded Advisor.
